```{r}
#| label: setup
#| include: false
library(tidyverse)

# The JPMorgan card-segment data used all morning (simulated).
set.seed(1122)
n <- 120
unemp <- round(runif(n, 3, 9), 1)
util <- round(rnorm(n, 30, 8), 1)
tenure <- round(pmax(rnorm(n, 6, 2), 0.5), 1)
rewards <- round(runif(n, 20, 80))
nco <- round(
  0.8 +
    0.30 * unemp +
    0.04 * util -
    0.07 * tenure +
    0 * rewards +
    rnorm(n, 0, 0.8),
  2
)
segs <- tibble(nco, unemp, util, tenure, rewards)
reg <- lm(nco ~ unemp + util + tenure + rewards, data = segs)

# helper: draw a t density with shaded rejection regions
t_plot <- function(df, lo = NULL, hi = NULL, t_obs = NULL) {
  d <- tibble(x = seq(-4.5, 4.5, length.out = 600), y = dt(x, df))
  p <- ggplot(d, aes(x, y)) +
    geom_line(linewidth = 1)
  if (!is.null(lo)) {
    p <- p +
      geom_area(data = filter(d, x <= lo), fill = "#E74C3C", alpha = 0.5)
  }
  if (!is.null(hi)) {
    p <- p +
      geom_area(data = filter(d, x >= hi), fill = "#E74C3C", alpha = 0.5)
  }
  if (!is.null(t_obs)) {
    p <- p + geom_vline(xintercept = t_obs, linetype = "dashed", linewidth = 1)
  }
  p + labs(x = "t", y = NULL) + theme_minimal(base_size = 15)
}
```

## The job: JPMorgan Chase, Consumer Card Risk

You are on a **card loss forecasting** team. Banks forecast losses for
reserves and for regulatory stress tests, so the team needs to know which
portfolio features move charge-offs.

| Variable | Meaning | Units |
|---|---|---|
| `nco` | **net charge-off rate**: share of balances written off as lost | % per year |
| `unemp` | local unemployment rate | % |
| `util` | average credit utilization | % |
| `tenure` | average account age | years |
| `rewards` | share of accounts that are rewards cards | % |

One row = one **portfolio segment** (a region × product group). $n = 120$.

::: {.callout-warning appearance="minimal"}
Simulated data. The setting is realistic; the numbers are invented.
:::

::: {.notes}
Thirty seconds of context, no more. A charge-off is a loan the bank gives up
on and writes off as a loss. Unemployment is the classic macro driver in loss
models, which is why stress-test scenarios are written in terms of the
unemployment rate.

Ask her to predict a sign for each variable before we fit anything. Write
her guesses on the board. Those guesses become the one-sided hypotheses on
slide 11. Unemp: plus. Util: plus. Tenure: minus (seasoned accounts have
already survived the risky early years). Rewards: no idea.
:::

## Multiple regression

$$
\text{nco}_i = \beta_0 + \beta_1\,\text{unemp}_i + \beta_2\,\text{util}_i
+ \beta_3\,\text{tenure}_i + \beta_4\,\text{rewards}_i + u_i
$$

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
**Same OLS idea**: pick the $\hat\beta$'s that minimize $\sum \hat u_i^2$.
Same sums of squares: $TSS = ESS + SSR$.

**New meaning**: $\beta_1$ is the change in nco for a one-point rise in
unemployment, **holding util, tenure, and rewards fixed** (S&W §6.2).
:::
::: {.column width="46%"}
**Degrees of freedom**: with $k$ regressors we estimate $k + 1$ coefficients,
so

$$
df = n - k - 1 = 120 - 4 - 1 = 115
$$

**Adjusted $R^2$** charges for each regressor:

$$
\bar R^2 = 1 - \frac{SSR/(n-k-1)}{TSS/(n-1)}
$$
:::
:::

::: {.notes}
Stock & Watson §6.2-6.4. Three things carry over from Thursday unchanged:
OLS minimizes squared misses, TSS = ESS + SSR, R^2 = ESS/TSS. Two things are
new: "holding fixed" and k.

On Thursday n - 2 was really n - k - 1 with k = 1. Point that out; it is the
same rule.

Adjusted R^2: R^2 can only go up when you add a regressor, even a useless
one. Adjusted R^2 can go down. That is all she needs.
:::

## The fitted model

```{r}
#| label: full-summary
summary(reg)
```

::: {.notes}
Do not explain anything yet. Let her look at it for twenty seconds. Ask:
"Which numbers can you already explain from Thursday?" She should find
Estimate, Std. Error, Residual standard error, Multiple R-squared, and the
degrees of freedom.

Everything else (t value, Pr(>|t|), the stars, the F-statistic) is today.
:::

## The $t$-test, in four steps

To test whether one coefficient equals some value $\beta_{j,0}$ (usually 0):

1. **State the hypotheses** *before* looking at the estimate:
   $H_0: \beta_j = \beta_{j,0}$ against $H_1$.
2. **Compute the $t$-statistic**: how many standard errors the estimate is from the null value
   $$
   t = \frac{\hat\beta_j - \beta_{j,0}}{SE(\hat\beta_j)}
   $$
3. **Find the $p$-value**: if $H_0$ were true, how likely is a $t$ at least this extreme?
4. **Decide**: reject $H_0$ if $p < \alpha$ (usually $\alpha = 0.05$), or
   equivalently if $t$ is beyond the critical value.

. . .

When $\beta_{j,0} = 0$, the $t$-statistic is just
$\hat\beta_j / SE(\hat\beta_j)$. That is R's `t value` column.

::: {.notes}
Stock & Watson §5.1 and §7.1. This is the same recipe as Day 9 (10/8) with a
mean; now the estimate is a slope. Say that, because she already did this.

Why t and not the normal: we estimated the SE, which adds a little extra
uncertainty. The t with n-k-1 degrees of freedom accounts for it (S&W §5.6).
With 115 df the t is very close to the normal, so 1.98 is close to 1.96.

The p-value definition is where people go wrong. It is NOT the probability
that H0 is true. It is the probability of data this extreme IF H0 were true.
Make her say it back.
:::

## Two-sided test: "is $\beta_j$ different from zero?"

$H_0: \beta_j = 0 \quad$ vs. $\quad H_1: \beta_j \neq 0 \qquad$ An estimate
far out in **either** direction is evidence against $H_0$.

```{r}
#| label: two-sided-plot
#| echo: false
#| fig-width: 10
#| fig-height: 3.2
#| fig-align: center
t_plot(115, lo = qt(0.025, 115), hi = qt(0.975, 115)) +
  annotate("text", x = -3.3, y = 0.08, label = "2.5%", size = 6) +
  annotate("text", x = 3.3, y = 0.08, label = "2.5%", size = 6)
```

$$
p = 2 \times P\big(T > |t|\big) \qquad \text{Reject at 5\% if } |t| > t_{0.975,\,df} = 1.98 \text{ (for 115 df)}
$$

In R: `2 * pt(-abs(t), df)` gives the $p$-value; `qt(0.975, df)` gives the
critical value.

::: {.notes}
The red area is the 5% we are willing to be wrong in, split in half because
we are watching both directions.

R's Pr(>|t|) column is ALWAYS this two-sided p-value. That fact matters for
the next slide.
:::

## You Try 1 — Two-sided tests by hand

From the table: `util` has estimate $0.037788$, SE $0.010551$.
`tenure` has estimate $-0.071478$, SE $0.042057$. $\;df = 115$,
$\;t_{0.975,\,115} = 1.98$.

**(a)** Test $H_0: \beta_{\text{util}} = 0$ against $H_1: \beta_{\text{util}} \neq 0$
at the 5% level. Compute $t$ and decide.

**(b)** Do the same for `tenure`.

**(c)** R reports $p = 0.092$ for `tenure`. Write one sentence that says what
this number means, without the words "probability that $H_0$ is true."

::: {.notes}
Five minutes.

(c) is the important one. A good answer: "If average account age truly had
no effect on charge-offs, we would see an estimate at least this far from
zero, in either direction, about 9% of the time."
:::

## Solution 1

**(a)** $t = 0.037788 / 0.010551 = 3.58$. $\;|3.58| > 1.98$ →
**reject** $H_0$. Utilization is significantly related to charge-offs at
5%. ($p = 0.0005$)

**(b)** $t = -0.071478 / 0.042057 = -1.70$. $\;|-1.70| < 1.98$ →
**fail to reject** $H_0$ at 5%. ($p = 0.092$)

**(c)** If tenure truly had **no** effect, an estimate at least 1.70 standard
errors from zero, in either direction, would happen about **9.2%** of the time.

. . .

::: {.callout-important appearance="minimal"}
"Fail to reject" is **not** "accept." We have not shown $\beta_{\text{tenure}} = 0$;
we have shown the data are not strong enough to rule it out.
:::

::: {.notes}
Hold on tenure. She predicted a negative sign. The estimate IS negative. The
two-sided test still says "not significant." Ask her: is that fair, given
that we only ever expected one direction? That question is the next slide.
:::

## One-sided test: "is $\beta_j$ *negative*?"

If theory says the sign **before** you see the data (seasoned accounts default
less), test only that direction:

$H_0: \beta_{\text{tenure}} = 0 \quad$ vs. $\quad H_1: \beta_{\text{tenure}} < 0$

```{r}
#| label: one-sided-plot
#| echo: false
#| fig-width: 10
#| fig-height: 3
#| fig-align: center
t_plot(115, lo = qt(0.05, 115), t_obs = -1.70) +
  annotate("text", x = -3.3, y = 0.08, label = "5%", size = 6) +
  annotate("text", x = -1.25, y = 0.36, label = "t = -1.70", size = 5)
```

| $H_1$ | $p$-value | Reject at 5% if | R |
|---|---|---|---|
| $\beta_j < 0$ (left tail) | $P(T < t)$ | $t < -1.66$ | `pt(t, df)` |
| $\beta_j > 0$ (right tail) | $P(T > t)$ | $t > 1.66$ | `pt(t, df, lower.tail = FALSE)` |

::: {.notes}
Stock & Watson §5.1, one-sided hypotheses. All 5% now sits in ONE tail, so
the cutoff moves in from 1.98 to 1.66.

Two rules to say out loud:
1. The direction comes from theory, chosen BEFORE seeing the estimate.
   Choosing the tail after seeing the sign is cheating; it doubles your real
   error rate.
2. When the estimate has the predicted sign, the one-sided p is half of R's
   two-sided p. When it has the WRONG sign, the one-sided p is 1 minus half,
   which is huge. R never prints the one-sided p; you compute it.
:::

## You Try 2 — One-sided tests

$df = 115$, $\;t_{0.95,\,115} = 1.66$.

**(a)** Test $H_1: \beta_{\text{tenure}} < 0$ at 5%. Use $t = -1.70$ from
You Try 1. What is the $p$-value? (Hint: R's two-sided $p$ was 0.092.)
Compare your decision with You Try 1(b).

**(b)** `unemp` has $t = 7.01$. Test $H_1: \beta_{\text{unemp}} > 0$.

**(c)** `rewards` has estimate $+0.0033$, two-sided $p = 0.485$. Someone
claims rewards cards *lower* losses: $H_1: \beta_{\text{rewards}} < 0$.
What is the one-sided $p$?

**(d)** The team's old model assumed $\beta_{\text{unemp}} = 0.25$. Test
$H_0: \beta_{\text{unemp}} = 0.25$ vs. $H_1: \beta_{\text{unemp}} \neq 0.25$
(estimate $0.334698$, SE $0.047718$).

::: {.notes}
Eight minutes.

(c) is the trap. The estimate points the wrong way. The one-sided p is not
0.24; it is 1 - 0.485/2 = 0.76. Data pointing the other way cannot be
evidence for your direction.

(d) is the first time the null is not zero. Same formula, just subtract
0.25 in the numerator. This matters in practice: you often test against an
old model's number, not against zero.
:::

## Solution 2

**(a)** Estimate has the predicted sign, so $p = 0.092/2 = 0.046$. Also
$t = -1.70 < -1.66$. **Reject** at 5%. The two-sided test did not reject;
the one-sided test does, because all 5% sits in the tail theory pointed to.

**(b)** $t = 7.01 > 1.66$ → reject. $p = P(T > 7.01) \approx 8 \times 10^{-11}$.
Higher unemployment goes with higher charge-offs.

**(c)** The estimate points the **wrong way**, so $p = 1 - 0.485/2 = 0.757$.
No evidence at all for $H_1$.

**(d)** $t = (0.334698 - 0.25)/0.047718 = 1.77$. $\;|1.77| < 1.98$ →
fail to reject. The data are consistent with the old model's 0.25.

::: {.notes}
(a) is the headline. Same data, same estimate, different conclusion, because
the question was different. That is why the hypothesis is written down before
the regression is run.

(d) Also notice: unemp is significantly different from 0 AND not
significantly different from 0.25. Both are true at once. A test answers the
question you asked.
:::

## Confidence intervals

A 95% confidence interval for $\beta_j$ (S&W §5.2):

$$
\hat\beta_j \;\pm\; t_{0.975,\,df} \times SE(\hat\beta_j)
$$

`tenure`: $\;-0.0715 \pm 1.98 \times 0.0421 = (-0.155,\; 0.012)$

. . .

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="48%"}
**The link to testing:** 0 is inside the interval ⇔ the two-sided test at 5%
does **not** reject $\beta_j = 0$.

The interval is every null value the data cannot reject.
:::
::: {.column width="48%"}
**Interpretation:** across repeated samples, 95% of intervals built this way
contain the true $\beta_j$.

It is *not* "a 95% chance the true value is in this particular interval."
:::
:::

`confint(reg)` prints them all.

::: {.notes}
The interval for tenure barely includes 0, matching the two-sided p of 0.09.
The interval for unemp, (0.24, 0.43), includes 0.25. That is You Try 2(d)
again, read off an interval instead of a t-stat.

Bayesian contrast, since she just did Bayes: the "95% chance it's in here"
reading is what a Bayesian credible interval says. A frequentist interval
does not say it. One sentence; do not reopen Block IV.
:::

## Testing several coefficients at once

The team asks: *do the two portfolio-mix variables, `tenure` and `rewards`,
matter at all, once we know unemployment and utilization?*

$$
H_0: \beta_{\text{tenure}} = 0 \text{ and } \beta_{\text{rewards}} = 0
\qquad H_1: \text{at least one is not } 0
$$

. . .

**Why not two $t$-tests?** Each has a 5% false-alarm rate. Running two of
them, the chance that *at least one* false-alarms is close to 10%, not 5%
(S&W §7.2). We need **one** test for the joint claim.

. . .

The **$F$-statistic** compares two models' sums of squared residuals:

$$
F = \frac{(SSR_{\text{restricted}} - SSR_{\text{unrestricted}})\,/\,q}{SSR_{\text{unrestricted}}\,/\,(n - k - 1)}
$$

- **Unrestricted**: the full model, all 4 regressors
- **Restricted**: the model with $H_0$ imposed (drop `tenure` and `rewards`)
- $q$ = number of restrictions (here 2); $\;k$ and $n - k - 1$ from the unrestricted model

::: {.notes}
Stock & Watson §7.2, the homoskedasticity-only F-statistic. The textbook
also gives a robust version; R's anova() computes this one.

Intuition, in one breath: dropping variables always makes the fit worse
(SSR goes up). The question is whether it gets worse by MORE than you would
expect if those variables were useless. The numerator is "how much worse,
per restriction." The denominator is "how much noise there is, per degree of
freedom." Big ratio = the dropped variables were doing real work.

Under H0, F follows an F distribution with q and n-k-1 degrees of freedom.
She met the F on Day 4. This is where it lives.
:::

## The $F$ at the bottom of every table

`summary()` always reports one particular $F$-test: **are all the slopes zero?**

$$
H_0: \beta_1 = \beta_2 = \cdots = \beta_k = 0
$$

The restricted model is just an intercept, which predicts $\bar Y$ for
everyone, so $SSR_{\text{restricted}} = TSS$. Then
$TSS - SSR = ESS$ and the formula becomes

$$
F = \frac{ESS / k}{SSR / (n - k - 1)}
$$

. . .

- `F-statistic: 16.6 on 4 and 115 DF` → $q = k = 4$, denominator df $= 115$
- **With one regressor, $F = t^2$.** Thursday's portfolio: $(-12.68)^2 = 160.8$,
  the F in its table.

::: {.notes}
This is the "overall F" or "regression F." It is rarely the interesting test
(of course SOMETHING matters), but she needs to be able to rebuild it. The
homework asks for it.

F = t^2 with one regressor: you are testing one restriction, so the joint
test and the single test are the same test. The homework asks her to verify
this numerically.
:::

## You Try 3 — The $F$-test by hand

$n = 120$, $\;k = 4$.

| Model | Regressors | SSR |
|---|---|---|
| Unrestricted | unemp, util, tenure, rewards | 93.361 |
| Restricted | unemp, util | 96.284 |

**(a)** Compute $F$ for $H_0: \beta_{\text{tenure}} = \beta_{\text{rewards}} = 0$.
What are $q$ and the denominator df?

**(b)** The 5% critical value is $F_{0.95}(2, 115) = 3.07$. Decide.

**(c)** The full model's $ESS = 53.899$. Compute the overall $F$ and check it
against the table.

::: {.notes}
Seven minutes.

(b) The joint test fails to reject. Yet the one-sided test on tenure
rejected. Not a contradiction: the joint test is two-sided in spirit and
spreads its attention over two variables, one of which (rewards) is pure
noise. Rewards dilutes tenure's signal. Say this; it is a real lesson about
bundling a weak variable with a dead one.
:::

## Solution 3

**(a)** $q = 2$, denominator df $= 120 - 4 - 1 = 115$.

$$
F = \frac{(96.284 - 93.361)/2}{93.361/115} = \frac{1.4615}{0.8118} = 1.80
$$

**(b)** $1.80 < 3.07$ → **fail to reject**. Together, tenure and rewards do
not significantly improve the model. ($p = 0.170$)

**(c)**
$$
F = \frac{53.899/4}{93.361/115} = \frac{13.475}{0.8118} = 16.6
$$
which matches `F-statistic: 16.6 on 4 and 115 DF`.

::: {.notes}
Everything on this slide is the homework's Question 3, with different
numbers. If she can do this slide she can do the homework.

Break here.

# Hour 2 · Code

## Every number in `summary()`, mapped

::: {style="font-size: 80%;"}
| Line in R | Symbol | Formula |
|---|---|---|
| `Estimate` | $\hat\beta_j$ | OLS ($S_{xy}/S_{xx}$ with one $X$) |
| `Std. Error` | $SE(\hat\beta_j)$ | $SER/\sqrt{S_{xx}}$ with one $X$ |
| `t value` | $t$ | $\hat\beta_j / SE(\hat\beta_j)$ |
| Pr(>&#124;t&#124;) | two-sided $p$ | `2 * pt(-abs(t), n - k - 1)` |
| stars | | \*\*\* below 0.001 · \*\* below 0.01 · \* below 0.05 · . below 0.1 |
| `Residual standard error: … on 115 degrees of freedom` | $SER$, $\;n-k-1$ | $\sqrt{SSR/(n-k-1)}$ |
| `Multiple R-squared` | $R^2$ | $ESS/TSS$ |
| `Adjusted R-squared` | $\bar R^2$ | $1 - \dfrac{SSR/(n-k-1)}{TSS/(n-1)}$ |
| `F-statistic: … on 4 and 115 DF` | overall $F$ | $\dfrac{ESS/k}{SSR/(n-k-1)}$ |
| `p-value` (last line) | $p$ for $F$ | `pf(F, k, n - k - 1, lower.tail = FALSE)` |
:::

::: {.notes}
This is the homework's reference card. Tell her to screenshot it.

The stars are a convenience, not a finding. A coefficient with p = 0.051
and one with p = 0.049 are essentially the same evidence; one gets a star,
one does not.
:::

## Every number in `anova()`, mapped

```{r}
#| label: anova-full
anova(reg)
```

- Each regressor row's `Sum Sq` is what that variable **adds**, given the rows
  above it. The rows **add up to ESS**.
- `Residuals` row: `Sum Sq` $= SSR$; `Df` $= n-k-1$; `Mean Sq` $= SSR/(n-k-1) = SER^2$.
- $TSS$ is not printed: add the whole `Sum Sq` column.
- `Mean Sq` $=$ `Sum Sq` / `Df`. `F value` $=$ row `Mean Sq` / Residuals `Mean Sq`.

::: {.notes}
Order matters for the individual rows (they are "sequential" sums of
squares) but not for their total. If she reorders the regressors, the rows
change and the sum does not. You can demonstrate in ten seconds by refitting
with rewards first. Do not go deeper; the homework has one regressor, where
this subtlety disappears.
:::

## What the table will not tell you

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="48%"}
**Standard errors assume constant spread.** R's default SEs are
*homoskedasticity-only*: they assume the spread of $u$ is the same at every
$X$. Stock & Watson recommend **robust** SEs that drop that assumption
(§5.4). Same estimates, slightly different SEs. You will meet them in
upper-level econometrics.
:::
::: {.column width="48%"}
**Significant ≠ causal.** A small $p$ says the association is unlikely to be
luck. It says nothing about *why*. Unemployment and charge-offs could both be
driven by a third thing. R prints `***` either way.

**Significant ≠ important.** With enough data, a tiny effect gets a tiny $p$.
Always read the **size** of the estimate.
:::
:::

::: {.notes}
Two minutes. These are guardrails, not new material. The causal point
connects back to Thursday's FICO/utilization note: FICO is partly computed
from utilization, so that slope cannot be read as a cause.
:::

## The segments, simulated

```{r}
#| label: sim-show
#| eval: false
set.seed(1122)
n <- 120
unemp <- round(runif(n, 3, 9), 1)
util <- round(rnorm(n, 30, 8), 1)
tenure <- round(pmax(rnorm(n, 6, 2), 0.5), 1)
rewards <- round(runif(n, 20, 80))
nco <- round(
  0.8 +
    0.30 * unemp +
    0.04 * util -
    0.07 * tenure +
    0 * rewards +
    rnorm(n, 0, 0.8),
  2
)
segs <- tibble(nco, unemp, util, tenure, rewards)
reg <- lm(nco ~ unemp + util + tenure + rewards, data = segs)
```

```{r}
#| label: sim-peek
head(segs, 3)
```

Look at the truth we wrote down. Do not tell the regression.

::: {.notes}
Point at the "0 * rewards". We built a variable with NO effect on purpose.
The table gave it p = 0.49. That is the test working.

And tenure: truly -0.07, but the two-sided test missed it. That is a Type II
error, live. Worth naming: the test was not wrong, it was underpowered. 120
segments was not enough to see an effect that small clearly.
:::

Then: build the 95% CI for `tenure` from `b`, `se`, and `crit_two`, and

::: {.notes}
Seven minutes. Every blank is a formula from Hour 1.
:::

## Solution 4

```{r}
#| label: you-try-4-soln
ct <- coef(summary(reg))
df_resid <- reg$df.residual

b <- ct["tenure", "Estimate"]
se <- ct["tenure", "Std. Error"]

t_stat <- b / se
p_two <- 2 * pt(-abs(t_stat), df_resid)
p_left <- pt(t_stat, df_resid)
crit_two <- qt(0.975, df_resid)
crit_one <- qt(0.05, df_resid)

round(
        c(
                t = t_stat,
                p_two = p_two,
                p_left = p_left,
                crit_two = crit_two,
                crit_one = crit_one
        ),
        4
)
round(
        rbind(
                by_hand = b + c(-1, 1) * crit_two * se,
                confint = confint(reg)["tenure", ]
        ),
        4
)
```

::: {.notes}
crit_one is -1.66 because qt(0.05, ...) is the LEFT tail. She may have
written qt(0.95, ...) and gotten +1.66; both are fine as long as she knows
which tail she is in. Make her say which.
:::

## You Try 5 — The $F$-test, two ways

```{r}
#| label: you-try-5
#| eval: false
reg_r <- lm(nco ~ unemp + util, data = segs) # H0 imposed

SSR_u <- sum(resid(reg)^2)
SSR_r <- sum(resid(____)^2)
q <- ____
df_u <- reg$df.residual

F_stat <- ((____ - ____) / q) / (____ / df_u)
p_F <- pf(F_stat, q, df_u, lower.tail = FALSE)
round(c(F = F_stat, p = p_F), 4)

anova(reg_r, reg) # R's version: restricted first, then unrestricted
```

**Then:** is the result consistent with what we *know* the truth to be?

::: {.notes}
Seven minutes. anova() with TWO models does exactly the F-test from slide
15. Have her find SSR_r and SSR_u in its output (column "RSS"; R's name for
SSR).

The truth question: rewards is truly 0, tenure is truly -0.07. So H0 is
FALSE (tenure is not zero), yet we failed to reject. Another Type II error,
caused by bundling tenure with a dead variable. Reveal the full truth now:
0.30, 0.04, -0.07, 0. Put the estimates next to it.
:::

## Solution 5

```{r}
#| label: you-try-5-soln
reg_r <- lm(nco ~ unemp + util, data = segs)
SSR_u <- sum(resid(reg)^2)
SSR_r <- sum(resid(reg_r)^2)
q <- 2
df_u <- reg$df.residual
F_stat <- ((SSR_r - SSR_u) / q) / (SSR_u / df_u)
round(
        c(
                SSR_r = SSR_r,
                SSR_u = SSR_u,
                F = F_stat,
                p = pf(F_stat, q, df_u, lower.tail = FALSE)
        ),
        4
)
anova(reg_r, reg)
```

$H_0$ is actually **false** here (the true tenure effect is $-0.07$), but
$F = 1.80$ does not reject. Bundling a real-but-small effect with a useless
variable hid it. That is a **Type II error**.

## Solution 6

```{r}
#| label: you-try-6-soln
a <- anova(reg)
SS <- a$`Sum Sq`
k <- 4
n <- nrow(segs)
ESS <- sum(SS[1:4])
SSR <- SS[5]
TSS <- ESS + SSR
R2 <- ESS / TSS
adjR2 <- 1 - (SSR / (n - k - 1)) / (TSS / (n - 1))
SER <- sqrt(SSR / (n - k - 1))
F_all <- (ESS / k) / (SSR / (n - k - 1))
round(
        c(
                TSS = TSS,
                ESS = ESS,
                SSR = SSR,
                R2 = R2,
                adjR2 = adjR2,
                SER = SER,
                F = F_all
        ),
        4
)
pf(F_all, k, n - k - 1, lower.tail = FALSE)
```

Every number matches the bottom of `summary(reg)`.

## Regression on one page

| Question | Tool | Statistic | Reject at 5% when |
|---|---|---|---|
| Is $\beta_j \neq 0$? | two-sided $t$ | $\hat\beta_j / SE$ | $\lvert t \rvert > 1.98$ ($df = 115$) |
| Is $\beta_j > 0$ (or $< 0$)? | one-sided $t$ | same $t$ | $t > 1.66$ (or $t < -1.66$) |
| Is $\beta_j \neq c$? | $t$ with a nonzero null | $(\hat\beta_j - c)/SE$ | $\lvert t \rvert > 1.98$ |
| Range of plausible $\beta_j$ | 95% CI | $\hat\beta_j \pm 1.98\,SE$ | 0 outside the CI |
| Do several $\beta$'s matter jointly? | $F$-test | $\dfrac{(SSR_r - SSR_u)/q}{SSR_u/(n-k-1)}$ | $F > F_{0.95}(q, n-k-1)$ |
| Does anything matter? | overall $F$ | $\dfrac{ESS/k}{SSR/(n-k-1)}$ | p-value $< 0.05$ |

# Appendix: the same thing in Python {visibility="uncounted"}

::: {.notes}
NOT part of the count. Do not present.
:::

## $t$, $p$, and $F$ in Python {visibility="uncounted"}

```python
import numpy as np
import statsmodels.formula.api as smf
import statsmodels.api as sm
from scipy import stats

reg   = smf.ols("nco ~ unemp + util + tenure + rewards", data=segs).fit()
reg_r = smf.ols("nco ~ unemp + util", data=segs).fit()

print(reg.summary())               # the summary(lm()) equivalent
sm.stats.anova_lm(reg)             # the anova() equivalent (sequential SS)

# t and p by hand for tenure
t = reg.params["tenure"] / reg.bse["tenure"]
df = reg.df_resid
p_two  = 2 * stats.t.sf(abs(t), df)
p_left = stats.t.cdf(t, df)

# the joint F-test, two ways
F = ((reg_r.ssr - reg.ssr) / 2) / (reg.ssr / df)
p_F = stats.f.sf(F, 2, df)
reg.compare_f_test(reg_r)          # returns (F, p, q)
```

::: {.callout-warning appearance="minimal"}
`reg.ssr` is the sum of squared **residuals**, matching Stock & Watson.
`reg.ess` is the explained sum of squares.
:::
